nodes.label: Single-User, New-Outlook-Only Scope Decision
nodes.rationale: Audience is one user (the author) on their own devices, so managed deployment, enterprise signing, and fleet validation are deferred; scale is not a v1 engineering concern because the product is local, delegated, read-only, and has no hosted service. Classic Outlook is excluded so no second client code path is built or tested.

nodes.label: Gated Native-First Architecture
nodes.rationale: A Windows Widgets Board provider is the best match for a glanceable Windows experience, but requires packaging, COM activation, and lifecycle testing that cannot be assumed. The native surface is therefore conditional on Phase 0 gates, with a surface-agnostic core so a tray/popover fallback reuses the same auth, Graph, cache, and display models rather than requiring a rewrite.

nodes.label: GetWidgetInfos() provider startup recovery
nodes.rationale: A provider can be recycled or restarted by the host at any time, so the documented pattern of enumerating widget infos and rebuilding each instance's ID, definition, CustomState, and context is required for pinned instances to be restored without user interaction.

nodes.label: WidgetManager.UpdateWidget delivery call
nodes.rationale: A synchronous void call into the Widgets host with no documented timeout and no cancellation, so it is unbounded and a payload already handed to it cannot be retracted.

nodes.label: Provider Is the Sole Delivery Authority
nodes.rationale: With the lease cleared before delivery, two processes could otherwise call UpdateWidget concurrently and a slow older call could land after a newer commit; the generation compare guards the cache but cannot retract a delivered payload. Ordering must be established before the call, so only the provider delivers and the companion merely commits and signals. The provider is also the only process holding widget IDs and per-instance contexts.

nodes.label: Serialized Coalescing Delivery Worker
nodes.rationale: A depth-one pending marker collapses concurrent requests so no two UpdateWidget calls are in flight and there is no interleaving to order. The trigger carries no payload: each pass re-reads committed snapshot, generation, and tombstone so content is chosen at delivery time rather than request time.

nodes.label: Final Convergence, Not Retraction
nodes.rationale: Because an in-flight UpdateWidget cannot be recalled, the plan claims only that the final rendered content reflects the newest committed state. A transient render of pre-change content is possible when a wedged host delays an already-entered call, so the limitation is documented in the README rather than claimed away, and no stronger ordering claim is made unless Phase 0 demonstrates stronger host semantics.

nodes.label: Per-Operation Disclosure Tombstone
nodes.rationale: The mutation mutex cannot be the only path to a fail-closed state, because a wedged peer is exactly when fail-closed matters most. Disclosure-reducing changes therefore suppress before they commit, on a path needing no mutex. One file per operation named by GUID: a shared file cannot be safely reclaimed because 'read owner ID then delete if it matches' is not an atomic conditional delete. Each operation deletes only its own file, suppression is active while any file exists, and the effective mode is the strongest present, so no operation can weaken another's suppression.

nodes.label: Suppress First, Commit Second Ordering
nodes.rationale: Ordering suppression before the risky operation means the safe state is already in place when the operation is attempted, so a mutex timeout leaves safety intact rather than requiring a signal that cannot be sent. Logout awaits MSAL RemoveAsync, which would otherwise open a window where the provider knows nothing and still holds a valid cache.

nodes.label: Mutation Mutex (bounded, never held across await)
nodes.rationale: System.Threading.Mutex is thread-affine, so a named mutex held across awaited WAM or Graph work can fail to release even inside a correct try/finally. Its critical section is therefore entirely synchronous local work. Every acquisition uses WaitOne(timeout) with a 2-second bound; the parameterless overload is prohibited because an indefinite wait behind a wedged peer has no recovery path.

nodes.label: Refresh Lease Record (cross-process single-flight)
nodes.rationale: Single-flight is expressed as an expiring record rather than a held lock so nothing is owned while WAM or Graph work is awaited. Crash recovery falls out for free: a killed owner leaves an expired record reclaimed by expiry alone, with no AbandonedMutexException dependence and no watchdog. A named Semaphore would avoid thread affinity but not the crash problem.

nodes.label: Boot-Session Discriminator for Lease Expiry
nodes.rationale: Expiry uses Environment.TickCount64, which is per-boot monotonic, so a stale post-reboot record could look live. Windows exposes no managed boot-identity API, so bootStamp = UtcNow minus TickCount64, quantized to 10 seconds, is derived instead. It fails safe: a clock step shifts the stamp and causes an early reclaim, never a stale lease appearing live.

nodes.label: 20-Second Async Refresh Deadline
nodes.rationale: A single linked cancellation source covering token acquisition, Graph requests, and validation. It deliberately does not bound the commit, which is synchronous and non-cancellable once entered, because cancelling between temp write and atomic replace is exactly how a half-committed state and a stranded release would occur.

nodes.label: 30-Second Lease Horizon
nodes.rationale: The horizon must exceed the ~27-second worst-case refresh transaction total, not just the async deadline. A lease expiring mid-commit would let a peer start a second refresh whose commit races the first; the generation compare prevents corruption but the wasted request and confusing indicator state are avoidable by choosing the horizon correctly.

nodes.label: Refresh Transaction (claim through lease clear)
nodes.rationale: Widget delivery is deliberately excluded from the transaction because UpdateWidget is unbounded and would otherwise drag the operation past the lease horizon, letting the lease be reclaimed under its own owner. Clearing the lease before delivery is safe: once the snapshot is committed and its generation incremented, a peer finds fresh data and skips under the 60-second activation rule.

nodes.label: ProtectedCache (DPAPI snapshot store)
nodes.rationale: Reads are lock-free and open the snapshot with FileShare.ReadWrite | FileShare.Delete so a Windows replace can proceed while a reader holds the prior file open; the reader observes either the prior or the new complete snapshot, never a partial one, and never waits on token acquisition or Graph I/O. The cache is reconstructible, so there is no migration path: on corruption or unsupported version, delete and refetch.

nodes.label: Snapshot Generation Counter
nodes.rationale: Re-comparing the captured account and state generation under the mutation mutex before committing stops an in-flight request from resurrecting data after logout or overwriting a newer setting. It guards the cache only; it cannot retract a delivered widget payload.

nodes.label: Bounded Atomic Replace Retry Ladder
nodes.rationale: Unrelated handles from antivirus, indexing, or a debugger can cause sharing violations during replacement, so retry at most three times at 25/50/100 ms while retaining the mutex; this keeps the non-cancellable critical section bounded by construction rather than by a token.

nodes.label: AbandonedMutexException Recovery
nodes.rationale: A process killed mid-commit abandons the mutex. The exception means the caller acquired it, so treat protected state as suspect, remove orphaned temp files, validate committed state and any lease record, then proceed or refetch, releasing in finally. The lease needs no equivalent handling because a dead owner simply leaves a record that expires.

nodes.label: SilentAuthService (provider-safe, silent only)
nodes.rationale: MSAL can fall back to a browser when WAM is unavailable, and interactive WAM needs an interactive session, a visible parent window, and a user action — none of which a provider has. The provider therefore exposes only silent acquisition with a zero parent handle, has no reference to AcquireTokenInteractive, and fails closed to a sign-in-required or broker-unavailable card.

nodes.label: GraphMailClient
nodes.rationale: Graph is called directly with HttpClient and System.Text.Json rather than the generated SDK, because three small read-only requests do not justify materially increasing the dependency surface.

nodes.label: No-Metadata Logging Rule
nodes.rationale: The logging API accepts no sender, subject, tenant, account, link, token, raw payload, correlation ID, or exception-dump field at all. Enforcing this by API shape and code review avoids maintaining a growing redaction subsystem, and lets diagnostic export copy the same metadata-free log without a second filtering pipeline.

nodes.label: Delegated Mail.ReadBasic Permission
nodes.rationale: Least-privileged permission for the required folder and message reads: it excludes bodies, body previews, attachments, and extended properties. Mail.Read is rejected because it would permit body access that the privacy design prohibits, and User.Read is unnecessary because account display data comes from the MSAL authentication result.

nodes.label: WAM / MSAL Brokered Authentication
nodes.rationale: WAM owns refresh-token maintenance and supports Conditional Access, MFA, Windows Hello, and FIDO, so the app never writes tokens to its own files and access tokens exist only in process memory for the Graph call.

nodes.label: Single-Tenant Secretless Entra Registration
nodes.rationale: One public-client registration with no secret or certificate, implicit grant disabled, and no application permissions. A separate production registration is a multi-user concern; the author can self-consent so no administrator step sits on the critical path.

nodes.label: Approval/Consent-Required Authorization State
nodes.rationale: A tenant user-consent policy block surfaces during interactive Entra/MSAL authorization before any token exists, so no Graph call is made and no 403 is returned. It must be named separately from a Graph 403 or a policy change will be misdiagnosed as a permissions bug in the app.

nodes.label: Graph HTTP 403 Mailbox-Refused State
nodes.rationale: A 403 means a token was issued but the mailbox request was refused — a materially different diagnosis from consent never being granted.

nodes.label: Inbox Unread/Total Count Query
nodes.rationale: unreadItemCount is authoritative for the folder and includes all item types including meeting requests, so the adjacent message list is labelled separately and is not expected to reconcile item-for-item.

nodes.label: Newest Five Message Previews Query
nodes.rationale: Strict $select with $orderby receivedDateTime desc and $top=5; the client re-bounds to five even if a malformed response returns more. Absolute local short time/date is rendered rather than relative strings, because cached cards can outlive a label like '2 minutes ago'.

nodes.label: Optional Focused Unread Count
nodes.rationale: Reads @odata.count from a filtered count query rather than the returned message. It stays unavailable unless Phase 0 proves filter syntax acceptance, agreement with New Outlook, acceptable latency, and that no undocumented ConsistencyLevel header is needed; its failure never discards the two required results.

nodes.label: No Delta Queries or Change Notifications in v1
nodes.rationale: An initial delta round can require walking the Inbox to establish state, and maintaining a synchronized mailbox store is disproportionate to a five-message snapshot. Revisit only if refresh volume becomes significant, which one user will not produce. $batch is likewise deferred until measurement shows benefit.

nodes.label: Cached-First, Activation-Driven Refresh Model
nodes.rationale: Microsoft warns the active interval can be short and guarantees no recurring refresh interval, so the platform is not trusted to keep the provider alive. The five-minute timer is opportunistic only, and v1 installs no startup process, service, scheduled task, webhook, or hosted backend.

nodes.label: Counts-Only Privacy Rendering
nodes.rationale: Subjects and senders are visible to shoulder surfers, so the small widget size is always counts-only and a global hide-details toggle converts every size. After 24 hours without a successful refresh, details are suppressed rather than presenting old subjects as current.

nodes.label: Adaptive Cards Schema 1.5 Rendering
nodes.rationale: Chosen over the newer HTML-widget option because the layout is small and bounded; Adaptive Cards avoid an unnecessary browser-rendering layer and reduce script, dependency, and content-security concerns. Widget text is treated as untrusted: length-bound, control-character sanitized, and data-bound into a fixed template rather than interpolated into executable content.

nodes.label: Slot-Plus-Generation Message Action
nodes.rationale: Action.Execute carries only a bounded display slot and snapshot generation, never the webLink or message ID in card JSON or CustomState; the provider reloads the snapshot, rejects stale generations or invalid slots, and validates the HTTPS host allowlist before launching. Action.OpenUrl is not used in v1.

nodes.label: Graph webLink Message Open Path
nodes.rationale: Only the documented Graph webLink is opened through the system HTTPS handler; message IDs are never transformed into undocumented URLs and no claim is made that the link opens New Outlook. The URL is never logged because it can contain sensitive identifiers.

nodes.label: olk.exe New Outlook Launch Strategy
nodes.rationale: Treated as a Phase 0 compatibility test rather than a guaranteed contract: bare-command resolution, alias resolution, and package activation are compared and the least brittle demonstrated method wins. A versioned WindowsApps path is never hard-coded, no Inbox-selection switch is assumed, and Classic Outlook is never silently substituted.

nodes.label: Universal Product Gates (1, 8, 10)
nodes.rationale: Package install with certificate trust, WAM sign-in with self-consent, and Mail.ReadBasic access are surface-independent: the tray fallback is also a packaged MSIX using the same certificate and permission, so these failures break it equally. A failure stops the product pending a tenant or device-policy fix; it must not be routed into fallback work that cannot possibly fix it.

nodes.label: Native-Surface Gates (2-6, 9, 11)
nodes.rationale: Widget discovery and pinning, cold activation, lifecycle recovery, multi-instance rendering, Board-action companion launch, zero-HWND silent tokens, and cached-first refresh across recycle. A critical failure here is exactly what the tray/popover fallback exists for, because the same core runs behind a different surface.

nodes.label: Approved Web-Only Open Outlook Mode
nodes.rationale: Gate 7 spans both groups. If bare olk.exe never resolves, that degrades one action rather than invalidating the product, because the widget's value is glanceable counts and subjects and a web fallback already exists. Proceeding requires explicit Phase 0 review approval and a stated README limitation; it is never a silent substitution.

nodes.label: Tray/Popover Fallback Surface
nodes.rationale: Predictable process lifetime and refresh, straightforward Outlook launch, but not a true Widgets Board experience. Built only after a native gate fails and only as a minimal reviewed proof; both full surfaces are never maintained in v1.

nodes.label: Surface-Agnostic Core
nodes.rationale: Keeping auth, Graph, cache, and display models independent of the surface makes both the tray fallback and any Widgets-roadmap change a surface swap rather than a rewrite, and it is nearly free to preserve now.

nodes.label: Signed MSIX From First Build
nodes.rationale: Signing from the beginning is what exercises the real certificate-trust and sideload-policy path on a managed device, and it is the prerequisite for ever sharing the tool — even though Windows permits unsigned test packages in restricted scenarios.

nodes.label: Publisher Continuity Decision
nodes.rationale: Package identity derives from name plus publisher and the manifest Publisher must match the certificate Subject, so a later enterprise certificate with a different Subject produces a different identity that installs alongside rather than upgrading. The stated v1 position is to accept remove-and-reinstall while keeping the cheaper persistent-identity option alive for free; this must be a recorded choice made before the first install rather than a later discovery.

nodes.label: MSIX Persistent Identity Bridge
nodes.rationale: The documented mechanism for changing publisher while preserving identity, requiring both certificates in hand while the old one is still valid. Phase 0 owes only its preconditions — long certificate validity, retained key and Subject — because losing or lapsing the development certificate is what forecloses the option, not failing to build the bridge now.

nodes.label: Signature Timestamping Decision
nodes.rationale: Without a trusted counter-signature the signature becomes invalid at certificate expiry and a retained package can no longer be installed, silently invalidating the remove-then-install rollback runbook. An installed package keeps running after expiry, so the failure appears only at the moment rollback is needed; if timestamping is skipped, the rollback shelf life must be stated explicitly.

nodes.label: Remove-Then-Install Rollback Runbook
nodes.rationale: MSIX will not install a lower version over a higher one, so v1 rollback is remove then install the prior signed package, accepting the loss of widget pins and package-local state. Phase 4 verifies a retained package actually installs rather than assuming it.

nodes.label: Signing Key Kept Outside Repo and OneDrive
nodes.rationale: A private key in the project tree would be synced, exposing a credential. Keep it in CurrentUser\My or a dedicated non-synced path and never export a .pfx under the repository; the key is never a deployment artifact.

nodes.label: OneDrive-Backed Repository Location
nodes.rationale: Staying in place preserves development portability and keeps source and build paths inside the environment already authorized for the agent tooling. The repo is marked Always keep on this device so builds never depend on Files On-Demand hydration; sharing violations are recorded and retried after pausing sync, and relocation is a fallback only after recurring reproducible contention.

nodes.label: Deferred Intune/RMM Managed Deployment
nodes.rationale: Retained as the multi-user design but not built, piloted, or tested at one user; nothing in Phases 0-4 depends on it and it must be re-verified against current documentation before use because managed-deployment behavior changes faster than the rest of the plan.

nodes.label: Widgets Policy Preflight (AllowNewsAndInterests)
nodes.rationale: Device policy can disable the entire Widgets experience, in which case a native-only package can never appear. Preflight the CSP/GPO before any build work and report 'widgets disabled by policy' distinctly rather than installing something that cannot surface.

nodes.label: Phase 1 Slice 1 — Test-First Coordination Layer
nodes.rationale: Two processes mutating shared state is the normal architecture here, not an exceptional path, and its failure modes are stale account data on screen, a stranded logout, or a hang. Correctness is therefore established first and test-first, moving account-switch and logout correctness out of Phase 3 rather than adding new work; Phase 3 then does fault injection over a layer that already passes its tests.

nodes.label: Phase 0 Evidence Report
nodes.rationale: One report recording versions, policy, consent, signing decisions, and per-gate pass/fail labelled universal or native, so a future multi-user step does not have to rediscover it and Phase 1 cannot begin on unreviewed evidence.

nodes.label: Account Switching Unproven Without a Second Account
nodes.rationale: Same-account sign-out and sign-in validates logout, cache clearing, and reacquisition only; with no second identity there is nothing for data to leak between, so account switching and cross-account cache isolation must be recorded as untested and the never-merge-two-accounts rule treated as unproven.
